COSMIX ALGORİTMA

EKIMIMIZ
HAKKINDA Algoritma Akademi'den tutkulu ve yaratıcı bir ekipiz; bilim, teknoloji, yenilik ve uzay keşfiyle ilgileniyoruz.

ABOUT OUR PROJECT
SPACE MISSION SIMULATOR is an interactive educational game that lets players create their own space missions by choosing rockets, spacecraft, scientific tools, and mission goals.

OUR GOAL
To make space exploration fun, interactive, and educational.

CONTACT INFORMATION
Email: cosmix.explore@gmail.com
summary: Space Mission Simulator is a free, browser-based 3D game by team COSMIX that lets students design, launch and operate a complete space mission, from the first science question to the final evaluation. Players pick a mission to Earth orbit, the Moon or Mars, choose what scientists want to learn, and build a spacecraft from real subsystem types: bus, solar arrays, batteries, antennas, computer, navigation, propulsion and science instruments. Every choice has a cost. A simulation engine recalculates budget, mass, power and energy, fuel, data storage and downlink in real time, so trade-offs become visible: a sharper camera means more data, a bigger antenna, more power and a heavier rocket. Players choose an orbit, assemble a two-stage rocket whose thrust-to-weight ratio and delta-v come from the real rocket equation, and must pass a readiness review organized by NASA's four mission segments. After a 3D launch they run Mission Control: managing batteries through eclipses, sending data when Earth is in view and making decisions during solar flares or dust storms. A 100-point evaluation explains what worked and how to improve, so students learn engineering by experimenting and redesigning.
details:
What it does

Space Mission Simulator turns NASA's mission design process into a playable 3D adventure for students aged 9–12 (and anyone curious about spaceflight). In about 10–15 minutes a player takes a mission from idea to results:

  1. Mission and science goals: choose Earth Observer Satellite, Discover the Moon or Mars Science Explorer, then pick the science goals. The goals decide which instruments are needed, just like real mission requirements.
  2. Spacecraft workshop: assemble a 3D spacecraft from buses, solar arrays, batteries, antennas, flight computers, navigation sensors, thruster packs and instruments (cameras, spectrometer, temperature sensor, radar). Every part card previews its trade-offs in mass, cost, power and data.
  3. Orbit planning: compare low, sun-synchronous, elliptical and higher orbits: science detail vs. time in shadow vs. contact with Earth vs. the fuel needed to brake into orbit.
  4. Rocket workshop: combine engines, fuel tanks, side boosters, upper stages and nose cones. Thrust-to-weight ratio and delta-v are calculated with the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation.
  5. Readiness review: a checklist grouped by NASA's launch, space, ground and user segments. Red items block the launch and explain how to fix them.
  6. Launch and operations: a 3D launch, a transfer trajectory, orbit insertion and Mission Control: switch instruments and the antenna, keep the battery alive through eclipses, avoid filling data storage, and make decisions during events such as solar flares, Martian dust storms, space debris, lunar eclipses and antenna glitches.
  7. Evaluation: a 100-point score (objectives, science, resources, engineering, operations) with personal feedback, XP, ranks, achievements and a Science Journal of discovery cards with real NASA facts.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Makes abstract engineering trade-offs visible: a better camera produces more data, which needs more storage, a stronger antenna, more power and a heavier rocket.
  • There is no single "best" spacecraft. Several designs succeed with different strategies, and the most expensive parts are not automatically better.
  • Learning by experimenting: players fix failed reviews, replay and improve their design instead of taking a test.
  • Classroom-ready: runs in any modern browser, no installation or accounts, a low-graphics mode for school computers, Turkish and English interfaces, and no personal data is collected.

How we built it

  • TypeScript, React 18 and Vite; Three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei for all 3D scenes; postprocessing for bloom; Zustand for game state; Vitest with 52 automated tests; the Web Audio API for original synthesized sounds; hosted on Vercel.
  • A deterministic simulation engine kept separate from rendering: the rocket equation, thrust-to-weight checks, inverse-square solar power, battery energy (Wh) vs. power (W), data storage and downlink with planet occultation, fuel for orbit insertion, seeded random events and transparent scoring. Simplified game values are documented separately from real physics.
  • Realistic visuals built on NASA imagery: Blue Marble (Earth), Black Marble (city lights), LRO colour and LOLA elevation maps (Moon) and NASA 3D Resources maps (Mars, Venus, Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune and stars), plus custom shaders for Earth's night side, the atmosphere, the Sun and rocket plumes.

What makes it creative

The game follows NASA's real design process (identify needs and goals, define the concept and requirements, design, build and verify, implement) and turns JPL's Concept Maturity Levels into a kid-friendly "mission maturity" meter. A robot guide called KOZMO coaches first-time players, and every learning card links to its NASA source.

Factors we considered

Age-appropriate language and large controls; accessibility (status is never shown by colour alone, plus a reduced-motion option); honest science (real facts are labelled and sourced, while budgets and part values are clearly marked as fictional game values); performance on school computers; and child safety: the planned four-player multiplayer mode will use private room codes, team roles and predefined messages only.

Use of AI (Super Intelligence)

We used AI tools throughout this project: AI assistants (including Anthropic's Claude) helped us brainstorm, research, write and debug the code, draft and translate text, analyse data, and create our team logo, cover image and demo video. All AI-assisted work was reviewed and tested by our team. This is an independent educational project and is not endorsed by NASA.
